title: Portability and Cross-Platform Development
learning_outcomes: Describe when portability and cross-platform development is useful and what problem it does not solve.
Evaluate a small example against its stated constraints, standard version and implementation assumptions.
Select a test or tool that can provide evidence of correctness without treating one successful run as proof.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
Professional C++ work requires reproducible builds, diagnostics, tests, dependency hygiene, secure boundaries and measurement. A passing build alone is not proof of correctness.

Portability and Cross-Platform Development focuses on the decisions and observable behavior named by the subtopics below. The aim is to explain the rule, predict what a small program should do, and then confirm the result with a focused check.

Use compiler warnings, repeatable tests, static analysis and sanitizers as complementary signals; keep tool configuration under version control.

content_blocks.title: Minimal example: Portability and Cross-Platform Development
content_blocks.expected_output: data.txt (when no command-line argument is supplied)
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save as `example.cpp`. Compile using `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic example.cpp -o example; then run ./example (Windows: .\example.exe).` The CodeLeaf page shows reference output only; it does not execute C++ learner code.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the example, rebuild with the same standard and warning flags, and rerun the same input. If the example is nondeterministic or depends on platform support, record that constraint instead of expecting byte-for-byte identical output.
content_blocks.limitations: The built-in CodeLeaf page does not execute C++ in a sandbox. Compile local teaching examples only; arbitrary learner code requires a separately deployed isolated runner with CPU, memory, process, filesystem and network limits.
content_blocks.explanation: Use filesystem paths instead of hardcoded separators. File existence, permissions, encoding and case-sensitivity can still differ across platforms.

items.text: Compare the alternatives in Standard C++ Versus Platform APIs by their semantics, constraints and trade-offs; use the simpler option that satisfies the real requirement.

items.title: Compiler Differences
items.text: A compiler translates source according to a selected language mode and target; diagnostics and supported features vary by toolchain version.

items.title: Paths and Filesystems
items.text: std::filesystem models paths and filesystem operations; paths and permissions vary by platform and every operation may fail.

items.title: Testing on Multiple Platforms
items.text: A test makes an expected behavior executable; useful suites include boundary and failure cases, not only successful examples.

content_blocks.title: Guided practice
content_blocks.text: Before changing the example, predict the output and name the rule that produces it. Then modify one line to demonstrate standard c++ versus platform apis, and add a test for one boundary or failure scenario. Keep the experiment small enough that another learner can reproduce it.

content_blocks.title: Version, safety and portability note
content_blocks.text: This topic may depend on newer C++ language or library support; this example uses a C++20-compatible illustration. Feature support varies by compiler version and standard-library implementation. Check the references and prefer explicit diagnostics to assumptions.

content.task: Extend the example for Portability and Cross-Platform Development with one additional valid case and one boundary or failure case. State your expected result first, then compile with the documented C++20 warning flags.
task_acceptance_criteria: The code compiles in the documented standard mode with warnings enabled.
The predicted output matches the actual result for the added case.
One relevant boundary, lifetime, portability or error case is tested or documented.
hints: Start by isolating the central rule from Portability and Cross-Platform Development.
Trace values or object lifetimes before changing the program.
Use a small boundary test and check the compiler diagnostic rather than assuming the behavior.
summary: Portability and Cross-Platform Development is about a concrete language rule or engineering decision, not only terminology.
Keep the important preconditions and trade-offs visible when applying portability and cross-platform development.
Use explicit build settings and focused tests to support the claim that the example behaves as expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming one successful example proves every case.
common_mistakes.why: It may miss an invalid input, boundary, error path or implementation difference.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the preconditions and test at least one ordinary case plus an edge or failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a language feature without checking its requirements.
common_mistakes.why: The code may depend on a standard version, an object lifetime or an API precondition.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the explicit standard mode and verify the relevant rule and compiler/library support.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring compiler diagnostics or simplifying away ownership and error behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Warnings and explicit contracts often expose a defect before it becomes a runtime problem.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with warnings, keep the smallest reproducible sample and state what happens when an operation fails.
